etymology: Hebrew shobal, of uncertain sense, perhaps “flowing” or “wandering,” the name of a son of Seir the Horite and a duke of that ancient people.
biblical_def: Shobal was a son of Seir the Horite, one of those whose names are set down in the register of the people who dwelt in the land of Seir before the children of Esau succeeded them (Gen 36:20). He is reckoned among the dukes of the Horites, the chieftains of the children of Seir in the land of Edom (Gen 36:29), and the dictionary records him as a real man of a real people whom the LORD planted in a mountain land long before. His children are named in the careful manner of the Scripture: “Alvan, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shepho, and Onam” (Gen 36:23). The chronicler gathered the same line again, that no name should be lost out of the book of the generations (1Ch 1:38,40). Shobal stands among the Horites who once held Mount Seir and were afterward dispossessed, for the LORD gave that land to Esau for a possession (Deu 2:12). The reader who meets his name learns that the rise of one nation and the fall of another is no chance of history but the appointment of God, who hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation (Act 17:26). Shobal had his hour and his dukedom, and then his people passed away; and the Scripture writes him down that we may number our own days, and remember that the LORD alone abideth for ever.

etymology: Hebrew tsib’on, perhaps “dyed” or “hyena,” the name of a son of Seir the Horite and a duke of that people.
biblical_def: Zibeon was a son of Seir the Horite, set down among the sons who inhabited the land of Seir before the children of Esau came to possess it (Gen 36:20). He is numbered with the dukes of the Horites, the chieftains of the children of Seir in the land of Edom (Gen 36:29). The Scripture names his children: “both Ajah, and Anah: this was that Anah that found the mules in the wilderness, as he fed the asses of Zibeon his father” (Gen 36:24). So Zibeon is remembered chiefly as the father of that Anah whose strange labor in the wilderness is marked for memory, and through Anah he is grandfather to Aholibamah, who became a wife of Esau (Gen 36:25). The chronicler gathered his name again into the book of generations, that the line of Seir might be kept entire (1Ch 1:38,40). Zibeon belonged to the Horites who held Mount Seir aforetime and were afterward destroyed and succeeded by the children of Esau (Deu 2:22). The dictionary records him to witness that the families of the earth are known and numbered of God, who divided to the nations their inheritance and set the bounds of the people (Deu 32:8). Zibeon fed his asses and ruled his dukedom in a mountain land now passed away; yet his name endures in the book, that we may learn how the LORD remembers the small histories of men while He governs the great history of the world.

etymology: Hebrew anah, perhaps “answering” or “one who answers,” the name of a son of Zibeon the Horite, remembered for a discovery in the wilderness.
biblical_def: Anah was a son of Zibeon, of the Horites who dwelt in the land of Seir, and he holds a singular place in the register of his people, for the Scripture marks him with a memory borne by no other: “this was that Anah that found the mules in the wilderness, as he fed the asses of Zibeon his father” (Gen 36:24). The word rendered “mules” is read by many as the hot springs of the desert, so that Anah is remembered as the man who, in the lowly task of feeding his father’s asses, came upon the warm waters of the wilderness. The children of Anah were Dishon, and Aholibamah his daughter (Gen 36:25), and this Aholibamah became a wife of Esau, so that through Anah the Horite blood mingled with the line of Edom (Gen 36:2). The chronicler kept his name in the book of generations (1Ch 1:40,41). The dictionary records Anah to witness that the LORD orders even the discoveries of a herdsman, and that no honest labor is beneath the notice of His providence. As Anah fed the asses he found a gift of waters in a dry land; and the reader may learn that the God who scattered springs in the desert of Seir is the same who leads His people beside the waters of comfort, and that diligence in a small calling is often the path to an unlooked-for mercy.

biblical_def: Dishon was a son of Seir the Horite, named among the sons who inhabited the land of Seir before the children of Esau possessed it (Gen 36:21). He is reckoned one of the dukes of the Horites, the chieftains of the children of Seir in the land of Edom (Gen 36:30). The Scripture sets down his children: “Hemdan, and Eshban, and Ithran, and Cheran” (Gen 36:26). There is also a Dishon who was a son of Anah, of the same people (Gen 36:25), so that the name is borne by more than one of the Horites; the careful reader marks the kinship without confusing the men. The chronicler gathered the line again into the book of generations (1Ch 1:38,41). Dishon belonged to that ancient people whom the LORD planted in Mount Seir and afterward dispossessed, giving the land to Esau for an inheritance (Deu 2:12). The dictionary records him to witness that the LORD knows the names of the chieftains of the earth, even of a people now vanished, and that He governs the bounds of every habitation. Dishon held his dukedom as the wild gazelle of his name held the mountain, swift and free for a season; yet the swiftest of the earth’s princes cannot outrun the appointed end, for the nations rise and fall at the bidding of the God who abideth for ever.

etymology: Hebrew etser, “treasure” or “store,” the name of a son of Seir the Horite and a duke of that people, distinct from other men called Ezer.
biblical_def: Ezer was a son of Seir the Horite, named among the sons who inhabited the land of Seir before the children of Esau came to dwell there (Gen 36:21). He is reckoned one of the dukes of the Horites, the chieftains of the children of Seir in the land of Edom (Gen 36:30). The Scripture sets down his children: “Bilhan, and Zaavan, and Akan” (Gen 36:27). This Ezer of Seir is to be distinguished from other men of the same name in the sacred record — an Ezer of the tribe of Ephraim, and Ezers among the builders and singers of the later books — for the name “treasure” was a common one in Israel and beyond. The chronicler gathered the Horite line again into his book of generations (1Ch 1:38,42). Ezer belonged to that ancient people whom the LORD planted in Mount Seir and afterward dispossessed, giving the land to Esau (Deu 2:22). The dictionary records him to witness that the LORD treasures up the names of the chieftains of the earth, even of a people now passed away. His name means treasure, yet his store and his dukedom are long gone; and the reader may learn that the only abiding treasure is laid up where moth and rust do not corrupt, in the inheritance reserved by the God who keeps the bounds of every habitation.

etymology: Hebrew dishan, “antelope” or “threshing,” the name of the youngest son of Seir the Horite and a duke of that people.
biblical_def: Dishan was the youngest of the sons of Seir the Horite, named last among the sons who inhabited the land of Seir before the children of Esau possessed it (Gen 36:21). He is reckoned one of the dukes of the Horites, the chieftains of the children of Seir in the land of Edom (Gen 36:30). The Scripture sets down his children, a short and quiet line: “Uz, and Aran” (Gen 36:28). His name is near to that of his brother Dishon, the two so close that the careful reader must weigh the letters to keep them apart; both were dukes of the Horites, sons of one father in Mount Seir. The chronicler gathered the line again into his book of generations, writing Dishan among the sons of Seir (1Ch 1:38,42). Dishan belonged to that ancient people whom the LORD planted in Seir and afterward dispossessed, giving the land to Esau for a possession (Deu 2:12). The dictionary records him, the youngest and least conspicuous of his house, to witness that the LORD overlooks none of the families of the earth. Though his line was short and his fame was small, his name is kept in the book of the living God; and the reader may learn that the providence which orders the great empires bends also over the least and last of men, numbering even the youngest son of a vanished people.

etymology: Hebrew chori, “cave-dweller” or “Horite,” the name of a son of Lotan, the eldest son of Seir, after whom the Horites are named.
biblical_def: Hori was a son of Lotan, who was the eldest son of Seir the Horite, and his name is bound up with the very name of his people, for the Horites are the children of Seir who dwelt in the caves and clefts of their mountain land (Gen 36:22). The Scripture names him with his brother: “And the children of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; and Lotan’s sister was Timna” (Gen 36:22). The chronicler kept the same in the book of generations (1Ch 1:39). This Hori, son of Lotan, is to be distinguished from another Hori of a far later age, the father of Shaphat the Simeonite who was sent to spy out the land of Canaan (Num 13:5). The Horites of Seir were an ancient people, met already in the days of Abraham, when Chedorlaomer smote “the Horites in their mount Seir” (Gen 14:6); and the LORD afterward gave their land to the children of Esau, who destroyed them from before them and dwelt in their stead (Deu 2:12). The dictionary records Hori, who bore the name of his whole people, to witness that the LORD raises up and removes the nations at His will. The cave-dwellers of Seir held their rocky strongholds for a season, yet no fastness of the mountains could shelter them from the hand that determines the bounds of habitation; and the reader is taught that the rock of true refuge is the LORD alone.

etymology: Hebrew heymam, also written Homam, perhaps “destroying” or “raging,” the name of a son of Lotan and brother of Hori.
biblical_def: Hemam was a son of Lotan, the eldest son of Seir the Horite, and the brother of Hori, named together in the register of that ancient people: “And the children of Lotan were Hori and Hemam; and Lotan’s sister was Timna” (Gen 36:22). When the chronicler gathered the same line into his book of generations, the name is written Homam (1Ch 1:39), one of those small variations of spelling that pass between the books of Moses and the Chronicles, and that the careful reader learns to recognize as the same man under a slightly altered form. Hemam belonged to the Horites of Mount Seir, the cave-dwellers whom the LORD planted in that land aforetime and afterward dispossessed, giving their inheritance to the children of Esau (Deu 2:22). The dictionary records him, a quiet name with no deeds of his own set down, to witness that the LORD keeps the genealogies of even the obscurest of men. Hemam did nothing that the Scripture saw fit to recount, yet his name is preserved in two books of the canon, that we may know the families of Seir were real and that God numbered them. The reader is taught that fame among men is not the measure of being known to God; the LORD who registered Hemam among the sons of Lotan keeps a far surer book, the book of life, wherein the names of His own are written that shall never be blotted out.

etymology: Hebrew alvan, also written Alian, perhaps “tall” or “lofty,” the name of a son of Shobal the Horite.
biblical_def: Alvan was a son of Shobal, who was himself a son of Seir the Horite and a duke of that people, and his name stands first in the list of Shobal’s children: “And the children of Shobal were these; Alvan, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shepho, and Onam” (Gen 36:23). When the chronicler gathered the line into his book of generations, the name is written Alian (1Ch 1:40), one of those small differences of spelling that pass between the books of Moses and the Chronicles, the v and the i exchanged, yet the same man meant under either form. Alvan belonged to the Horites of Mount Seir, the people whom the LORD planted in that land aforetime and afterward dispossessed, that the children of Esau might dwell in their stead (Deu 2:12). The dictionary records him, a name without recorded deed, to witness that the LORD numbers the grandsons of Seir as carefully as He numbers the princes of the earth. Alvan’s name may signify the lofty or the tall, yet whatever height his house attained, it was brought low when the Horites passed away. The reader is taught that the loftiness of man shall be bowed down, and the haughtiness of men shall be made low, and the LORD alone shall be exalted; for He who registered Alvan among the sons of Shobal abides when the proudest of the nations are forgotten.

etymology: Hebrew manachath, “rest” or “resting place,” the name of a son of Shobal the Horite; a place also bears the name.
biblical_def: Manahath was a son of Shobal, of the line of Seir the Horite, named second among Shobal’s children: “And the children of Shobal were these; Alvan, and Manahath, and Ebal, Shepho, and Onam” (Gen 36:23). The chronicler kept the same name in his book of generations (1Ch 1:40). This entry concerns the man; for there is also a place called Manahath, reckoned among the dwellings of the children of Benjamin and of certain families of Judah (1Ch 8:6), so that the careful reader distinguishes the person of Seir from the town of the later record. Manahath belonged to the Horites of Mount Seir, the people whom the LORD planted in that land aforetime and afterward dispossessed, giving their inheritance to the children of Esau (Deu 2:22). The dictionary records him, a name that signifies rest, to witness that the LORD numbers the families of the earth even when their own histories are silent. Manahath’s name speaks of rest, yet his people found no abiding rest in Mount Seir, for they were destroyed from before the children of Esau and dwelt there no more. The reader is taught that there remaineth a rest for the people of God which no earthly mountain can give, a rest that is not in any land of this passing world but in the LORD Himself, who is the everlasting habitation of His people, the same yesterday, today, and for ever.
